Indeed, the bearing of this impressive woman, throughout the day, was a
      pattern to all impressive women under similar circumstances. She renewed
      the acquaintance of Mr and Mrs Boffin, as if Mr and Mrs Boffin had said of
      her what she had said of them, and as if Time alone could quite wear her
      injury out. She regarded every servant who approached her, as her sworn
      enemy, expressly intending to offer her affronts with the dishes, and to
      pour forth outrages on her moral feelings from the decanters. She sat
      erect at table, on the right hand of her son-in-law, as half suspecting
      poison in the viands, and as bearing up with native force of character
      against other deadly ambushes. Her carriage towards Bella was as a
      carriage towards a young lady of good position, whom she had met in
      society a few years ago. Even when, slightly thawing under the influence
      of sparkling champagne, she related to her son-in-law some passages of
      domestic interest concerning her papa, she infused into the narrative such
      Arctic suggestions of her having been an unappreciated blessing to
      mankind, since her papa’s days, and also of that gentleman’s having been a
      frosty impersonation of a frosty race, as struck cold to the very soles of
      the feet of the hearers. The Inexhaustible being produced, staring, and
      evidently intending a weak and washy smile shortly, no sooner beheld her,
      than it was stricken spasmodic and inconsolable. When she took her leave
      at last, it would have been hard to say whether it was with the air of
      going to the scaffold herself, or of leaving the inmates of the house for
      immediate execution. Yet, John Harmon enjoyed it all merrily, and told his
      wife, when he and she were alone, that her natural ways had never seemed
      so dearly natural as beside this foil, and that although he did not
      dispute her being her father’s daughter, he should ever remain stedfast in
      the faith that she could not be her mother’s.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Extended portrait of Mrs Wilfer's bearing throughout the day—masterfully satirical depiction of her suspicious, imperious, and self-righteous conduct—followed by John Harmon's loving observation of how Bella's genuine nature shines by contrast.

# Context

This passage concludes a scene in which Eugene Wrayburn passionately declares his commitment to remain in society with his wife Lizzie and fight for her openly, rather than hide away in shame. Behoves Mortimer Lightwood, therefore, to answer a dinner card from Mr and
      Mrs Veneering requesting the honour, and to signify that Mr Mortimer
      Lightwood will be happy to have the other honour. The Veneerings have
      been, as usual, indefatigably dealing dinner cards to Society, and whoever
      desires to take a hand had best be quick about it, for it is written in
      the Books of the Insolvent Fates that Veneering shall make a resounding
      smash next week. Yes. Having found out the clue to that great mystery how
      people can contrive to live beyond their means, and having over-jobbed his
      jobberies as legislator deputed to the Universe by the pure electors of
      Pocket-Breaches, it shall come to pass next week that Veneering will
      accept the Chiltern Hundreds, that the legal gentleman in Britannia’s
      confidence will again accept the Pocket-Breaches Thousands, and that the
      Veneerings will retire to Calais, there to live on Mrs Veneering’s
      diamonds (in which Mr Veneering, as a good husband, has from time to time
      invested considerable sums), and to relate to Neptune and others, how
      that, before Veneering retired from Parliament, the House of Commons was
      composed of himself and the six hundred and fifty-seven dearest and oldest
      friends he had in the world. It shall likewise come to pass, at as nearly
      as possible the same period, that Society will discover that it always did
      despise Veneering, and distrust Veneering, and that when it went to
      Veneering’s to dinner it always had misgivings—though very secretly
      at the time, it would seem, and in a perfectly private and confidential
      manner.

When I devised this story, I foresaw the likelihood that a class of
      readers and commentators would suppose that I was at great pains to
      conceal exactly what I was at great pains to suggest: namely, that Mr John
      Harmon was not slain, and that Mr John Rokesmith was he. Pleasing myself
      with the idea that the supposition might in part arise out of some
      ingenuity in the story, and thinking it worth while, in the interests of
      art, to hint to an audience that an artist (of whatever denomination) may
      perhaps be trusted to know what he is about in his vocation, if they will
      concede him a little patience, I was not alarmed by the anticipation.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Dickens's authorial preface directly addresses readers' suspicions about John Harmon's identity, defending the novel's design as intentionally artful and asking for patience with serialized narrative. This metanarrative moment is essential for understanding the novel's construction and Dickens's artistic self-awareness.
enrichment.best_quote: I foresaw the likelihood that a class of readers and commentators would suppose that I was at great pains to conceal exactly what I was at great pains to suggest: namely, that Mr John Harmon was not slain, and that Mr John Rokesmith was he.
enrichment.summary: Dickens explains that he intentionally created ambiguity about John Harmon's identity and asks readers to trust his artistic judgment and patience with the serialized format.

context: This is not from Bleak House—it is from Charles Dickens's *Our Mutual Friend*. To keep for a long time unsuspected, yet always working itself out,
      another purpose originating in that leading incident, and turning it to a
      pleasant and useful account at last, was at once the most interesting and
      the most difficult part of my design. Its difficulty was much enhanced by
      the mode of publication; for, it would be very unreasonable to expect that
      many readers, pursuing a story in portions from month to month through
      nineteen months, will, until they have it before them complete, perceive
      the relations of its finer threads to the whole pattern which is always
      before the eyes of the story-weaver at his loom. Yet, that I hold the
      advantages of the mode of publication to outweigh its disadvantages, may
      be easily believed of one who revived it in the Pickwick Papers after long
      disuse, and has pursued it ever since.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Dickens discusses the novel's central structural challenge: maintaining a secret plot thread across nineteen months of serialization while ensuring readers can ultimately perceive the pattern. This is a remarkable authorial commentary on narrative craft and the unique demands of serialized fiction.
enrichment.best_quote: To keep for a long time unsuspected, yet always working itself out, another purpose originating in that leading incident, and turning it to a pleasant and useful account at last, was at once the most interesting and the most difficult part of my design.
enrichment.summary: Dickens reflects on the difficulty of maintaining a secret subplot across serialized publication, defending the mode of publication despite its challenges.

There is sometimes an odd disposition in this country to dispute as
      improbable in fiction, what are the commonest experiences in fact.
      Therefore, I note here, though it may not be at all necessary, that there
      are hundreds of Will Cases (as they are called), far more remarkable than
      that fancied in this book; and that the stores of the Prerogative Office
      teem with instances of testators who have made, changed, contradicted,
      hidden, forgotten, left cancelled, and left uncancelled, each many more
      wills than were ever made by the elder Mr Harmon of Harmony Jail.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Dickens defends the plausibility of the will-related plot device by citing actual cases of testators' eccentric behavior in the Prerogative Office records. This demonstrates his commitment to grounding even extraordinary fiction in social reality.

enrichment.summary: Dickens argues that his fiction is grounded in real practice and cites the Prerogative Office records as proof that his plot devices are less extraordinary than actual legal cases.

In my social experiences since Mrs Betty Higden came upon the scene and
      left it, I have found Circumlocutional champions disposed to be warm with
      me on the subject of my view of the Poor Law. My friend Mr Bounderby could
      never see any difference between leaving the Coketown ‘hands’ exactly as
      they were, and requiring them to be fed with turtle soup and venison out
      of gold spoons. Idiotic propositions of a parallel nature have been freely
      offered for my acceptance, and I have been called upon to admit that I
      would give Poor Law relief to anybody, anywhere, anyhow. Putting this
      nonsense aside, I have observed a suspicious tendency in the champions to
      divide into two parties; the one, contending that there are no deserving
      Poor who prefer death by slow starvation and bitter weather, to the
      mercies of some Relieving Officers and some Union Houses; the other,
      admitting that there are such Poor, but denying that they have any cause
      or reason for what they do. The records in our newspapers, the late
      exposure by  The Lancet , and the common sense and senses of common people,
      furnish too abundant evidence against both defences. But, that my view of
      the Poor Law may not be mistaken or misrepresented, I will state it. I
      believe there has been in England, since the days of the  Stuarts , no law
      so often infamously administered, no law so often openly violated, no law
      habitually so ill-supervised. In the majority of the shameful cases of
      disease and death from destitution, that shock the Public and disgrace the
      country, the illegality is quite equal to the inhumanity—and known
      language could say no more of their lawlessness.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Dickens's sustained polemical defense of his Poor Law critique is the chapter's most extensive social commentary, addressing critics directly and enumerating specific instances of illegality and inhumanity in the administration of relief. This passage crystallizes the novel's humanitarian social critique and Dickens's commitment to justice.
enrichment.best_quote: I believe there has been in England, since the days of the Stuarts, no law so often infamously administered, no law so often openly violated, no law habitually so ill-supervised. In the majority of the shameful cases of disease and death from destitution, that shock the Public and disgrace the country, the illegality is quite equal to the inhumanity—and known language could say no more of their lawlessness.
enrichment.summary: Dickens defends his critique of the Poor Law as grounded in observable fact and ethical principle, arguing it is the most infamously administered law in English history.

context: This is an author's preface or postscript reflecting on the novel's social commentary regarding the Poor Law and its administration in England. Dickens defends his portrayal of Mrs Betty Higden's character and his critique of how Poor Law relief is handled, arguing that the system has been consistently mismanaged and inhumanely administered.

On Friday the Ninth of June in the present year, Mr and Mrs Boffin (in
      their manuscript dress of receiving Mr and Mrs Lammle at breakfast) were
      on the South Eastern Railway with me, in a terribly destructive accident.
      When I had done what I could to help others, I climbed back into my
      carriage—nearly turned over a viaduct, and caught aslant upon the
      turn—to extricate the worthy couple. They were much soiled, but
      otherwise unhurt. The same happy result attended Miss Bella Wilfer on her
      wedding day, and Mr Riderhood inspecting Bradley Headstone’s red
      neckerchief as he lay asleep. I remember with devout thankfulness that I
      can never be much nearer parting company with my readers for ever, than I
      was then, until there shall be written against my life, the two words with
      which I have this day closed this book:—THE END.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Dickens's personal account of the Staplehurst railway accident and his miraculous escape—linking it to the fates of his fictional characters and ending with 'THE END'—is a profound and moving coda that merges the author's personal experience with the novel's themes of death, rescue, and redemption, adding existential weight to the narrative.
enrichment.best_quote: I remember with devout thankfulness that I can never be much nearer parting company with my readers for ever, than I was then, until there shall be written against my life, the two words with which I have this day closed this book:—THE END.
enrichment.summary: Dickens recounts his experience in the Staplehurst railway accident of June 9, 1865, expressing gratitude for his miraculous escape and reflecting on mortality in connection with the novel's conclusion.

Silas Wegg, being on his road to the Roman Empire, approaches it by way of
      Clerkenwell. The time is early in the evening; the weather moist and raw.

      and also that he feels it due to himself to be anxiously expected at the
      Bower. ‘Boffin will get all the eagerer for waiting a bit,’ says Silas,

Not, however, towards the ‘shops’ where cunning artificers work in pearls
      and diamonds and gold and silver, making their hands so rich, that the
      enriched water in which they wash them is bought for the refiners;—not

      candle dimly burning in it, surrounded by a muddle of objects vaguely
      resembling pieces of leather and dry stick, but among which nothing is
      resolvable into anything distinct, save the candle itself in its old tin
      candlestick, and two preserved frogs fighting a small-sword duel. Stumping
      with fresh vigour, he goes in at the dark greasy entry, pushes a little
      greasy dark reluctant side-door, and follows the door into the little dark
      greasy shop. It is so dark that nothing can be made out in it, over a

      upon the floor, and wiped the tears of laughter from her eyes.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Physical manifestation of Mrs Boffin's uninhibited joy through laughter and movement; demonstrates her unguarded, exuberant nature.
enrichment.summary: Mrs Boffin expresses her delight through unrestrained clapping, rocking, laughter, and tears of joy.

context: Mrs Boffin expresses her delight at the prospect of owning a fashionable carriage and living in high society now that she and Mr Boffin have come into a great fortune. Her enthusiastic description of the yellow chariot, footman, coachman, and bay horses fills her with such glee that she bursts into uncontrollable laughter.

chapter_title: MR AND MRS BOFFIN IN CONSULTATION
text:
‘And what, my old lady,’ inquired Mr Boffin, when he also had
      sympathetically laughed: ‘what’s your views on the subject of the Bower?’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Functional question that transitions to the next topic of discussion; no substantive content.
enrichment.summary: Mr Boffin asks Mrs Boffin about her views on the Bower.

context: Mr. Boffin asks his wife for her views on what to do with the Bower, their old residence, after they've inherited a great fortune and decided to embrace fashionable society and move to a better house in a good neighborhood.

chapter_title: MR AND MRS BOFFIN IN CONSULTATION
text: ‘Shut it up. Don’t part with it, but put somebody in it, to keep it.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mrs Boffin's practical decision about the old property is straightforward and shows prudent stewardship; minor character trait.
enrichment.summary: Mrs Boffin proposes shutting up the Bower while keeping it and installing a caretaker.

context: Mrs Boffin suggests what should be done with the Bower (their old home) now that they have inherited a great fortune and plan to move to fashionable society. She proposes closing it up while retaining ownership and hiring someone to maintain it.

chapter_title: MR AND MRS BOFFIN IN CONSULTATION
text: ‘Any other views?’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Routine prompting question; purely functional dialogue.
enrichment.summary: Mr Boffin invites Mrs Boffin to share additional views.

context: The Boffins discuss how to use their newfound fortune. After Mrs. Boffin expresses her desire for fashionable society and describes her fantasy of owning a grand carriage, Mr. Boffin asks if she has additional plans for their wealth and lifestyle.

chapter_title: MR AND MRS BOFFIN IN CONSULTATION
text:
‘Noddy,’ said Mrs Boffin, coming from her fashionable sofa to his side on
      the plain settle, and hooking her comfortable arm through his, ‘Next I
      think—and I really have been thinking early and late—of the
      disappointed girl; her that was so cruelly disappointed, you know, both of
      her husband and his riches. Don’t you think we might do something for her?
      Have her to live with us? Or something of that sort?’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mrs Boffin's compassionate proposal to assist Bella Wilfer is a pivotal moment revealing her benevolence and establishing a major plot thread; her tender consideration is deeply affecting.
enrichment.best_quote: Don't you think we might do something for her? Have her to live with us? Or something of that sort?
enrichment.summary: Mrs Boffin, moved by Bella Wilfer's disappointment at losing both husband and fortune, proposes they invite her to live with them.

context: Mrs Boffin proposes to Mr Boffin that they invite a disappointed girl who lost both her husband and his riches to live with them, as part of their plans to do good with their newfound fortune.

chapter_title: MR AND MRS BOFFIN IN CONSULTATION
text:
‘Ne-ver once thought of the way of doing it!’ cried Mr Boffin, smiting the
      table in his admiration. ‘What a thinking steam-ingein this old lady is.
      And she don’t know how she does it. Neither does the ingein!’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mr Boffin's admiration for his wife's wisdom is expressed through playful metaphor ('thinking steam-engine'); reveals his character and their marital affection.
enrichment.best_quote: What a thinking steam-ingein this old lady is.
enrichment.summary: Mr Boffin expresses his wonder at Mrs Boffin's thoughtful suggestion through affectionate teasing about her remarkable insight.

context: Mr. Boffin expresses admiration for his wife's clever suggestion to help the disappointed girl (Bella Wilfer) by inviting her to live with them, praising her intuitive wisdom and thoughtful ideas about how to use their newfound fortune generously.

chapter_title: MR AND MRS BOFFIN IN CONSULTATION
text:
Mrs Boffin pulled his nearest ear, in acknowledgment of this piece of
      philosophy, and then said, gradually toning down to a motherly strain:
      ‘Last, and not least, I have taken a fancy. You remember dear little John
      Harmon, before he went to school? Over yonder across the yard, at our
      fire? Now that he is past all benefit of the money, and it’s come to us, I
      should like to find some orphan child, and take the boy and adopt him and
      give him John’s name, and provide for him. Somehow, it would make me
      easier, I fancy. Say it’s only a whim—’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mrs Boffin's proposal to adopt an orphan child in memory of young John Harmon is profound and redemptive; it reveals her deepest values and plants a crucial plot seed regarding the mystery of the fortune.
enrichment.best_quote: Now that he is past all benefit of the money, and it's come to us, I should like to find some orphan child, and take the boy and adopt him and give him John's name, and provide for him.
enrichment.summary: Mrs Boffin proposes adopting an orphan child, naming him John Harmon in memory of the young heir who drowned, thereby using their inherited fortune for redemptive good.

context: Mrs Boffin outlines her plans for how the Boffins should use their newly inherited fortune. After discussing acquiring fashionable society and a grand carriage, she proposes her final and most heartfelt idea: to adopt an orphan child and name him after a dear child they once knew, John Harmon, as a way to honor that memory and do good with their newfound wealth.

chapter_title: MR AND MRS BOFFIN IN CONSULTATION
text: ‘But I don’t say so,’ interposed her husband.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Brief agreement with no substantive content; purely functional.
enrichment.summary: Mr Boffin denies that the proposal is merely a whim.

context: The Boffins discuss how to use their newfound fortune. Mrs. Boffin proposes adopting an orphan child in memory of a boy named John Harmon who died before benefiting from the money. Mr. Boffin agrees with his wife's charitable plan, responding that he would not dismiss her idea.

chapter_title: MR AND MRS BOFFIN IN CONSULTATION
text: ‘No, but deary, if you did—’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Incidental dialogue; no substantive content.
enrichment.summary: Mrs Boffin suggests a hypothetical objection that Mr Boffin is about to counter.

context: Mrs Boffin proposes adopting an orphan child in honor of a boy named John Harmon who died before he could benefit from the Boffins' newfound fortune. When her husband Mr Boffin expresses support for this charitable idea, Mrs Boffin playfully responds with this fragment, suggesting she trusts his judgment.

chapter_title: MR AND MRS BOFFIN IN CONSULTATION
text: ‘I should be a Beast if I did,’ her husband interposed again.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mr Boffin's emphatic and morally passionate response shows his character; demonstrates agreement through strong language.
enrichment.best_quote: I should be a Beast if I did
enrichment.summary: Mr Boffin emphatically rejects any notion that the adoption proposal is merely a whim, calling himself a beast if he doubted it.

context: The Boffins discuss how to use their newfound fortune. Mrs. Boffin proposes adopting an orphan child in memory of the young John Harmon, and her husband firmly agrees it would be wrong to refuse such a charitable act.

chapter_title: MR AND MRS BOFFIN IN CONSULTATION
text:
‘That’s as much as to say you agree? Good and kind of you, and like you,
      deary! And don’t you begin to find it pleasant now,’ said Mrs Boffin, once
      more radiant in her comely way from head to foot, and once more smoothing
      her dress with immense enjoyment, ‘don’t you begin to find it pleasant
      already, to think that a child will be made brighter, and better, and
      happier, because of that poor sad child that day? And isn’t it pleasant to
      know that the good will be done with the poor sad child’s own money?’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mrs Boffin's radiant affirmation of the adoption plan emphasizes the redemptive purpose of their fortune and their mutual joy; thematically rich and emotionally warm.
enrichment.best_quote: And isn't it pleasant to know that the good will be done with the poor sad child's own money?
enrichment.summary: Mrs Boffin joyfully affirms their plan and reflects on the beauty of using the drowned child's own money to benefit a living orphan.

context: Mrs Boffin persuades her husband to adopt an orphan child in memory of young John Harmon, arguing that using the inherited money to improve an orphan's life would honor the boy who died before the fortune came to them. She emphasizes the pleasure and moral satisfaction of doing good with the deceased child's own money.

chapter_title: MR AND MRS BOFFIN IN CONSULTATION
text:
‘Yes; and it’s pleasant to know that you are Mrs Boffin,’ said her
      husband, ‘and it’s been a pleasant thing to know this many and many a
      year!’ It was ruin to Mrs Boffin’s aspirations, but, having so spoken,
      they sat side by side, a hopelessly Unfashionable pair.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mr Boffin's tender declaration of love for his wife is interrupted by Dickens' authorial intrusion denouncing them as 'Unfashionable'—a pivotal moment reconciling the couple's virtue with society's judgment.
enrichment.best_quote: Yes; and it's pleasant to know that you are Mrs Boffin, and it's been a pleasant thing to know this many and many a year!
enrichment.summary: Mr Boffin lovingly affirms his wife's moral character, but Dickens narrates that their virtuous intentions doom their social aspirations to fashionability.

context: Mr. and Mrs. Boffin have just discussed their plans for their newfound fortune, including acquiring fashionable society and a grand carriage. Mrs. Boffin proposes adopting an orphan child in memory of young John Harmon. When her husband affirms his agreement and expresses his affection for her, he inadvertently undermines her fashionable aspirations with his sincere, humble sentiment, leaving them as an unfashionable couple despite their wealth.

chapter_title: MR AND MRS BOFFIN IN CONSULTATION
text:
These two ignorant and unpolished people had guided themselves so far on
      in their journey of life, by a religious sense of duty and desire to do
      right. Ten thousand weaknesses and absurdities might have been detected in
      the breasts of both; ten thousand vanities additional, possibly, in the
      breast of the woman. But the hard wrathful and sordid nature that had
      wrung as much work out of them as could be got in their best days, for as
      little money as could be paid to hurry on their worst, had never been so
      warped but that it knew their moral straightness and respected it. In its
      own despite, in a constant conflict with itself and them, it had done so.
      And this is the eternal law. For, Evil often stops short at itself and
      dies with the doer of it; but Good, never.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Dickens' authorial commentary elevates the Boffins' simple goodness to philosophical and moral grandeur; a profound statement about the nature of virtue, duty, and redemption central to the novel's themes.
enrichment.best_quote: For, Evil often stops short at itself and dies with the doer of it; but Good, never.
enrichment.summary: Dickens reflects that the Boffins, though ignorant and unpolished, have been guided by genuine religious duty and moral righteousness that even hardened souls cannot entirely resist.

context: Mr. and Mrs. Boffin, newly wealthy from an inheritance, discuss how to use their fortune virtuously. After deciding to adopt an orphan child and help a disappointed young woman, the narrator reflects on the couple's moral character despite their lack of polish and education, praising their fundamental goodness and sense of duty that even their former harsh employer recognized and respected.

chapter_title: MR AND MRS BOFFIN IN CONSULTATION
text:
Through his most inveterate purposes, the dead Jailer of Harmony Jail had
      known these two faithful servants to be honest and true. While he raged at
      them and reviled them for opposing him with the speech of the honest and
      true, it had scratched his stony heart, and he had perceived the
      powerlessness of all his wealth to buy them if he had addressed himself to
      the attempt. So, even while he was their griping taskmaster and never gave
      them a good word, he had written their names down in his will. So, even
      while it was his daily declaration that he mistrusted all mankind—and
      sorely indeed he did mistrust all who bore any resemblance to himself—he
      was as certain that these two people, surviving him, would be trustworthy
      in all things from the greatest to the least, as he was that he must
      surely die.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Dickens' meditation on the dead Jailer's (John Harmon Senior's) recognition of the Boffins' incorruptible honesty is thematically profound and plot-critical, revealing the dead man's judgment of character and his will.
enrichment.best_quote: he had perceived the powerlessness of all his wealth to buy them if he had addressed himself to the attempt
enrichment.summary: Dickens explains that old John Harmon, despite his misanthropy and greed, respected the Boffins' moral integrity so deeply that he named them in his will as trustees of his fortune.

context: This passage explains the backstory of how Mr. and Mrs. Boffin came to inherit their fortune. Despite being harsh and miserly during their years as servants to the wealthy but misanthropic "Jailer of Harmony Jail," he recognized their fundamental honesty and integrity. His respect for their moral character, which persisted even as he exploited them as workers, led him to bequeath them his wealth in his will—the fortune that now allows them to aspire to fashionable society.

chapter_title: MR AND MRS BOFFIN IN CONSULTATION
text:
Mr and Mrs Boffin, sitting side by side, with Fashion withdrawn to an
      immeasurable distance, fell to discussing how they could best find their
      orphan. Mrs Boffin suggested advertisement in the newspapers, requesting
      orphans answering annexed description to apply at the Bower on a certain
      day; but Mr Boffin wisely apprehending obstruction of the neighbouring
      thoroughfares by orphan swarms, this course was negatived. Mrs Boffin next
      suggested application to their clergyman for a likely orphan. Mr Boffin
      thinking better of this scheme, they resolved to call upon the reverend
      gentleman at once, and to take the same opportunity of making acquaintance
      with Miss Bella Wilfer. In order that these visits might be visits of
      state, Mrs Boffin’s equipage was ordered out.

enrichment.interest_rationale: The Boffins' practical discussion of finding an orphan is grounded and earnest, concluding with their decision to visit the clergyman and Bella Wilfer; advances plot and reveals character priorities.
enrichment.best_quote: Mrs Boffin's equipage was ordered out
enrichment.summary: The Boffins discuss practical methods of finding an orphan, dismissing newspaper advertisements due to potential chaos, and resolve to consult their clergyman while making a state visit to acquaint themselves with Bella Wilfer.

context:
# Context

After Mr. and Mrs. Boffin decide to adopt an orphan child in memory of young John Harmon, they discuss practical methods for finding a suitable candidate. This passage shows their deliberation process as they reject advertising in newspapers due to concerns about attracting too many applicants, then settle on consulting their clergyman for a recommendation. The passage concludes with their decision to make formal visits of state to both the clergyman and Miss Bella Wilfer, for which Mrs. Boffin's carriage is prepared.
